tasks.extracted: Meta-analysis of 34 prospective cohort studies published until December 2005 (publication years 1981 to 2005 in Table 2's subgroups): 56 dose-response curves, 1 015 835 participants and 94 533 deaths, each curve against its study's lowest-intake category, which was no alcohol intake with former drinkers excluded for 30 curves, and declared no alcohol use (12 curves) or occasional use (14) with former drinkers not excluded. Intake in grams a day; a drink as each study defined it, otherwise 10 g of ethanol (7 studies). The pooled fixed-effect curve was J-shaped: lowest mortality at 6 g a day, about half a drink, relative risk 0.81 (95% CI 0.80 to 0.83), a maximum reduction of 19% (17% to 20%); the association with lower mortality was apparent up to 42 g a day (about 4 drinks). A random-effects repeat gave a very similar curve with wider intervals (deviance 879.4 against 154.0), shown only in a figure.

tasks.extracted: The subgroups are drawn from the 107 studies of Zhao et al. (2023). The authors state that their lower, medium and higher categories of daily intake are too broad to define precisely the drinking levels at which mortality risk is significantly increased, that very few higher-quality studies meet their criteria, that many studies measured drinking over only the previous week or 2 or 3 days, and, citing the Canadian guidance work, that studies of alcohol and all-cause mortality are too prone to bias and confounding to form a sound basis for low-risk drinking guidelines. In Figure 2 (random study effect), the younger cohorts compared with lifetime abstainers rise from low to medium to higher intake (0.98, 1.17, 1.51 in Table 2), while the curve of the 18 studies of older cohorts with both abstainer biases dips at low volume (0.84 in Table 3) and does not rise clearly above 1 even at 45 g a day or more (read from the figure; its values are not printed).

Drinking has at least three dimensions (frequency, usual quantity per occasion, binge drinking) that correlate only partly and differ in their cardiovascular effects; genetic variants lower all three, so genetic analyses cannot separate them, and those linking intake-lowering variants to lower cardiovascular risk may be showing the harm of binge drinking. Genotype tests lifelong (and parental) rather than adult exposure; given common unhealthy drinking patterns in adolescence and early adulthood, their lower prevalence in young adults carrying ALDH2 variants, and the possibility that binge drinking starts atherosclerosis (a mouse study and a vascular-function study are cited), such analyses may be testing adult binge drinking and possibly also teenage and young-adult binge drinking, with uncertain relevance to limited drinking in mid-life.
